title: A grazing encounter between two spiral galaxies
caption: The spiral galaxies NGC 2207 and IC 2163, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: IC 2163, NGC 2207 · constellation Canis Major · about 110 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA/ESA and The Hubble Heritage Team (STScI)

recognition.text: Ranked #49 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Two spiral galaxies slip past each other like great ships in the night in this Hubble image, taken with the Wide Field Planetary Camera 2. They are NGC 2207 and IC 2163, about 110 million light-years away in the direction of the constellation Canis Major.

The pair are caught in a near-collision, a grazing encounter rather than a head-on crash. When galaxies come this close, each one's gravity pulls on the other's stars and gas, and over time such encounters can reshape both of them.

A spiral galaxy is a flattened disc of stars, gas and dust with arms winding out from a central region. NGC 2207 and IC 2163 are caught at a single moment in an interaction that unfolds over spans of time far longer than a human life, so one image cannot show the motion itself.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (4.82 x 2.47 arcminutes) and distance (110 million light years), the frame spans roughly 154,000 × 79,000 light-years. Its light set out about 110 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 observed from ultraviolet through visible to near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet and near-infrared parts of this light are invisible to the eye.
